name: Logon Event Types
location: %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\logs\Security.evtx — the Logon Type field within Event ID 4624
purpose: Determines by exactly what means a logon was attempted, in addition to date, time, username, hostname, and success/failure status — the single field that separates a console logon from a network logon, RDP session, or scheduled-task logon.
key_fields: Logon Type 7 — credentials used to unlock screen, or an RDP session reconnect
Logon Type 8 — network logon sending credentials in cleartext
Logon Type 9 — different credentials used than the logged-on user
Logon Type 11 — cached credentials used to logon
Logon Type 12 — cached remote interactive (similar to Type 10)
Logon Type 13 — cached unlock (similar to Type 7)
normal_baseline: Logon Type 2 for regular console users during business hours; Type 3 for expected file-share/network access; Type 10 only from known admin or remote-work sources.
anomalies: Logon Type 10 (RDP) from an unexpected source at an odd hour
Logon Type 8 (cleartext network credentials) appearing at all on a modern, properly configured network
Logon Type 9 (different credentials than the logged-on user) on a host with no legitimate reason for credential switching, consistent with pass-the-hash or RunAs abuse
Logon Type 5 (service logon) tied to an account that isn't a known service account
anti_forensic_notes: The Logon Type is only as trustworthy as the 4624 event itself — if Security-log auditing is disabled or the log is cleared, this classification is lost along with the rest of the logon record.
interpretation: Always read the Logon Type alongside the account name and source IP/workstation fields on the same 4624 event — the type alone tells you the *mechanism*, not whether the logon itself was legitimate. Use this table to disambiguate `successful-failed-logons` records and to interpret Type 10 correctly for `rdp-eventlogs` correlation.
